<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Zhenqin Wu
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Molecular machine learning has been maturing rapidly over the last few years. Improved methods and the presence of larger datasets have enabled machine learning algorithms to make increasingly accurate predictions about molecular properties. However, algorithmic progress has been limited due to the lack of a standard benchmark to compare the efficacy of proposed methods; most new algorithms are benchmarked on different datasets making it challenging to gauge the quality of proposed methods. This work introduces MoleculeNet, a large scale benchmark for molecular machine learning. MoleculeNet curates multiple public datasets, establishes metrics for evaluation, and offers high quality open-source implementations of multiple previously proposed molecular featurization and learning algorithms (released as part of the DeepChem open source library). MoleculeNet benchmarks demonstrate that learnable representations are powerful tools for molecular machine learning and broadly offer the best performance. However, this result comes with caveats. Learnable representations still struggle to deal with complex tasks under data scarcity and highly imbalanced classification. For quantum mechanical and biophysical datasets, the use of physics-aware featurizations can be more important than choice of particular learning algorithm.</p>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Overlap between chemistry and
statistical learning has had a long history. The field of cheminformatics has been utilizing machine learning methods in chemical modeling(e.g. quantitative structure activity relationships, QSAR) for decades.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gasteiger and Zupan (1993)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zupan and Gasteiger (1999)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Varnek and Baskin (2012)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mitchell (2014)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Devillers (1996)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schneider and Wrede (1998)</a></cite> In the recent 10 years, with the advent of sophisticated deep learning methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">LeCun et al. (2015)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmidhuber (2015)</a></cite>, machine learning has gathered increasing amounts of attention from the scientific community. Data-driven analysis has become a routine step in many chemical and biological applications, including virtual screening<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. (2015)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramsundar et al. (2015)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Unterthiner et al. (2014)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wallach et al. (2015)</a></cite>, chemical property prediction<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Delaney (2004)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lusci et al. (2013)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mobley et al. (2014)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mobley and Guthrie (2014)</a></cite>, and quantum chemistry calculations<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rupp et al. (2012)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Montavon et al. (2013)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schütt et al. (2016)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">McGibbon et al. (2017)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In many such applications, machine learning has shown strong potential to compete with or even outperform conventional <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ab-initio</span> computations<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mobley and Guthrie (2014)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Montavon et al. (2013)</a></cite>. It follows that introduction of novel machine learning methods has the potential to reshape research on properties of molecules. However, this potential has been limited by the lack of a standard evaluation platform for proposed machine learning algorithms. Algorithmic papers often benchmark proposed methods on disjoint dataset collections, making it a challenge to gauge whether a proposed technique does in fact improve performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Data for molecule-based machine learning tasks are highly heterogeneous and expensive to gather. Obtaining precise and accurate results for chemical properties typically requires specialized instruments as well as expert supervision (contrast with computer speech and vision, where lightly trained workers can annotate data suitable for machine learning systems). As a result, molecular datasets are usually much smaller than those available for other machine learning tasks. Furthermore, the breadth of chemical research means our interests with respect to a molecule may range from quantum characteristics to measured impacts on the human body. Molecular machine learning methods have to be capable of learning to predict this very broad range of properties. Complicating this challenge, input molecules can have arbitrary size and components, highly variable connectivity and many three dimensional conformers (three dimensional molecular shapes). To transform molecules into a form suitable for conventional machine learning algorithms (that usually accept fixed length input), we have to extract useful and related information from a molecule into a fixed dimensional representation (a process called featurization).<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rogers and Hahn (2010)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duvenaud et al. (2015)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kearnes et al. (2016)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To put it simply, building machine learning models on molecules requires overcoming several key issues: limited amounts of data, wide ranges of outputs to predict, large heterogeneity in input molecular structures and appropriate learning algorithms. Therefore, this work aims to facilitate the development of molecular machine learning methods by curating a number of dataset collections, creating a suite of software that implements many known featurizations of molecules, and providing high quality implementations of many previously proposed algorithms. Following the footsteps of WordNet<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Miller (1995)</a></cite> and ImageNet<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al. (2009)</a></cite>, we call our suite MoleculeNet, a benchmark collection for molecular machine learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In machine learning, a benchmark serves as more than a simple collection of data and methods. The introduction of the ImageNet benchmark in 2009 has triggered a series of breakthroughs in computer vision, and in particular has facilitated the rapid development of deep convolutional networks. The ILSVRC, an annual contest held by the ImageNet team<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Russakovsky et al. (2015)</a></cite>, draws considerable attention from the community, and greatly stimulates collaborations and competitions across the field. The contest has given rise to a series of prominent machine learning models such as AlexNet<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krizhevsky et al. (2012)</a></cite>, GoogLeNet<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Szegedy et al. (2014)</a></cite>, ResNet<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al. (2015)</a></cite> which have had broad impact on the academic and industrial computer science communities. We hope that MoleculeNet will trigger similar breakthroughs by serving as a platform for the wider community to develop and improve models for learning molecular properties.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In particular, MoleculeNet contains data on the properties of over 700,000 compounds. All datasets have been curated and integrated into the open source DeepChem package.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">dee ()</a></cite> Users of DeepChem can easily load all MoleculeNet benchmark data through provided library calls. MoleculeNet also contributes high quality implementations of well known (bio)chemical featurization methods. To facilitate comparison and development of new methods, we also provide high quality implementations of several previously proposed machine learning methods. Our implementations are integrated with DeepChem, and depend on Scikit-Learn <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pedregosa et al. (2011)</a></cite> and Tensorflow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abadi et al. (2016)</a></cite> underneath the hood. Finally, evaluation of machine learning algorithms requires defined methods to split datasets into training/validation/test collections. Random splitting, common in machine learning, is often not correct for chemical data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sheridan (2013)</a></cite>. MoleculeNet contributes a library of splitting mechanisms to DeepChem and evaluates all algorithms with multiple choices of data split. MoleculeNet provide a series of benchmark results of implemented machine learning algorithms using various featurizations and splits upon our dataset collections. These results are provided within this paper, and will be maintained online in an ongoing fashion as part of DeepChem.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The related work section will review prior work in the chemistry community on gathering curated datasets and discuss how MoleculeNet differs from these previous efforts. The methods section reviews the dataset collections, metrics, featurization methods, and machine learning models included as part of MoleculeNet. The results section will analyze the benchmarking results to draw conclusions about the algorithms and datasets considered.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MoleculeNet draws upon a broader movement within the chemical community to gather large sources of curated data. PubChem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bolton et al. (2008)</a></cite> and PubChem BioAssasy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2012)</a></cite> gather together thousands of bioassay results, along with millions of unique molecules tested within these assays. The ChEMBL database offers a similar service, with millions of bioactivity outcomes across thousands of protein targets. Both PubChem and ChEMBL are human researcher oriented, with web portals that facilitate browsing of the available targets and compounds. ChemSpider is a repository of nearly 60 million chemical structures, with web based search capabilities for users. The Crystallography Open Database <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gražulis et al. (2009)</a></cite> and Cambridge Structural Database <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Groom et al. (2016)</a></cite> offer large repositories of organic and inorganic compounds. The protein data bank <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Berman et al. (2003)</a></cite> offers a repository of experimentally resolved three dimensional protein structures. This listing is by no means comprehensive; the methods section will discuss a number of smaller data sources in greater detail.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These past efforts have been critical in enabling the growth of computational chemistry. However, these previous databases are not machine-learning focused. In particular, these collections don’t define metrics which measure the effectiveness of algorithmic methods in understanding the data contained. Furthermore, there is no prescribed separation of the data into training/validation/test sets (critical for machine learning development). Without specified metrics or splits, the choice is left to individual researchers, and there are indeed many chemical machine learning papers which use subsets of these data stores for machine learning evaluation. Unfortunately, the choice of metric and subset varies widely between groups, so two methods papers using PubChem data may be entirely incomparable. MoleculeNet aims to bridge this gap by providing benchmark results for a reasonable range of metrics, splits, and subsets of these (and other) data collections.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">It’s important to note that there have been some efforts to create benchmarking datasets for machine learning in chemistry. The Quantum Machine group <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qua ()</a></cite> and previous work on multitask learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramsundar et al. (2015)</a></cite> both introduce benchmarking collections which have been used in multiple papers. MoleculeNet incorporates data from both these efforts and significantly expands upon them.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methods</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MoleculeNet is based on the open source package DeepChem<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">dee ()</a></cite>. Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3 Methods ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows an annotated DeepChem benchmark script. Note how different choices for data splitting, featurization, and model are available. DeepChem also directly provides molnet sub-module to support benchmarking. The single line below runs benchmarking on the specified dataset, model and featurizer. User defined models capable of handling DeepChem datasets are also supported.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">MoleculeNet is based on the open source package DeepChem<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">dee ()</a></cite>. Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3 Methods ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows an annotated DeepChem benchmark script. Note how different choices for data splitting, featurization, and model are available. DeepChem also directly provides molnet sub-module to support benchmarking. The single line below runs benchmarking on the specified dataset, model and featurizer. User defined models capable of handling DeepChem datasets are also supported.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">deepchem.molnet.run_benchmark(datasets, model, split, featurizer)
</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we will further elaborate the benchmarking system, introducing available datasets as well as implemented splitting, metrics, featurization, and learning methods.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/benchmark_framework.png" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/179;" width="476" height="179" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Example code for benchmark evaluation with DeepChem, multiple methods are provided for data splitting, featurization and learning.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Datasets</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MoleculeNet is built upon multiple public databases. The full collection currently includes over 700,000 compounds tested on a range of different properties. These properties can be subdivided into four categories: quantum mechanics, physical chemistry, biophysics and physiology. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Datasets ‣ 3 Methods ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, separate datasets in the MoleculeNet collection cover various levels of molecular properties, ranging from molecular-level properties to macroscopic influences on human body. For each dataset, we propose a metric and a splitting pattern(introduced in the following texts) that best fit the properties of the dataset. Performances on the recommended metric and split are reported in the results section.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In most datasets, SMILES strings<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weininger (1988)</a></cite> are used to represent input molecules, 3D coordinates are also included in part of the collection as molecular features, which enables different methods to be applied. Properties, or output labels, are either 0/1 for classification tasks, or floating point numbers for regression tasks. At the time of writing, MoleculeNet contains 17 datasets prepared and benchmarked, but we anticipate adding further datasets in an on-going fashion. We also highly welcome contributions from other public data collections. For more detailed dataset structure requirements and instructions on curating datasets, please refer to the tutorial on DeepChem webpage.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Datasets ‣ 3 Methods ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> lists details of datasets in the collection, including tasks, compounds and their features, recommended splits and metrics. Contents of each dataset will be elaborated in this subsection.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/dataset_composition.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/156;" width="476" height="156" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Tasks in different datasets focus on different levels of properties of molecules.</figcaption>
</figure>

<td id="S3.T1.2.17.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T1.2.17.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">Random</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.17.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T1.2.17.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">ROC-AUC</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T1.2.18" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T1.2.18.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T1.2.18.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">ClinTox</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.18.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T1.2.18.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">SMILES</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.18.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T1.2.18.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">2</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.18.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T1.2.18.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">Classification</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.18.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T1.2.18.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">1491</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.18.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T1.2.18.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">Random</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.18.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S3.T1.2.18.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:50%;">ROC-AUC</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.1 </span>QM7/QM7b</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The QM7/QM7b datasets are subsets of the GDB-13 database<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Blum and Reymond (2009)</a></cite>, a database of nearly 1 billion stable and synthetically accessible organic molecules, containing up to seven “heavy” atoms (C, N, O, S). The 3D Cartesian coordinates of the most stable conformation and electronic properties (atomization energy, HOMO/LUMO eigenvalues, etc.) of each molecule were determined using <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ab-initio</span> density functional theory (PBE0/tier2 basis set).<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rupp et al. (2012)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Montavon et al. (2013)</a></cite> Learning methods benchmarked on QM7/QM7b are responsible for predicting these electronic properties given stable conformational coordinates. For the purpose of more stable performances as well as better comparison, we recommend stratified splitting(introduced in the next subsection) for QM7.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.2 </span>QM8</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The QM8 dataset comes from a recent study on modeling quantum mechanical calculations of electronic spectra and excited state energy of small molecules.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramakrishnan et al. (2015)</a></cite> Multiple methods, including time-dependent density functional theories (TDDFT) and second-order approximate coupled-cluster (CC2), are applied to a collection of molecules that include up to eight heavy atoms (also a subset of the GDB-17 database<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ruddigkeit et al. (2012)</a></cite>). In total, four exicted state properties are calculated by three different methods on 22 thousand samples.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.3 </span>QM9</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">QM9 is a comprehensive dataset that provides geometric, energetic, electronic and thermodynamic properties for a subset of GDB-17 database<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ruddigkeit et al. (2012)</a></cite>, comdprising 134 thousand stable organic molecules with up to nine heavy atoms<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramakrishnan et al. (2014)</a></cite>. All moleucles are modeled using density functional theory (B3LYP/6-31G(2df,p) based DFT). In our benchmark, geometric properties (atomic coordinates) are integrated into features, which are then applied to predict other properties.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The datasets introduced above (QM7, QM7b, QM8, QM9) were curated as part of the Quantum-Machine effort <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qua ()</a></cite>, which has processed a number of datasets to measure the efficacy of machine-learning methods for quantum chemistry.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.4 </span>ESOL</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ESOL is a small dataset consisting of water solubility data for 1128 compounds.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Delaney (2004)</a></cite> The dataset has been used to train models that estimate solubility directly from chemical structures (as encoded in SMILES strings).<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duvenaud et al. (2015)</a></cite> Note that these structures don’t include 3D coordinates, since solubility is a property of a molecule and not of its particular conformers.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS5" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.5 </span>FreeSolv</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Free Solvation Database (FreeSolv) provides experimental and calculated hydration free energy of small molecules in water<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mobley and Guthrie (2014)</a></cite>. A subset of the compounds in the dataset are also used in the SAMPL blind prediction challenge<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mobley et al. (2014)</a></cite>. The calculated values are derived from alchemical free energy calculations using molecular dynamics simulations. We include the experimental values in the benchmark collection, and use calculated values for comparison.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS6" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.6 </span>Lipophilicity</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Lipophilicity is an important feature of drug molecules that affects both membrane permeability and solubility. This dataset, curated from ChEMBL database,<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hersey (2015)</a></cite> provides experimental results of octanol/water distribution coefficient (logD at pH 7.4) of 4200 compounds.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS7" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.7 </span>PCBA</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">PubChem BioAssay (PCBA) is a database consisting of biological activities of small molecules generated by high-throughput screening.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2012)</a></cite> We use a subset of PCBA, containing 128 bioassays measured over 400 thousand compounds, used by previous work to benchmark machine learning methods.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramsundar et al. (2015)</a></cite></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS8" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.8 </span>MUV</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Maximum Unbiased Validation (MUV) group is another benchmark dataset selected from PubChem BioAssay by applying a refined nearest neighbor analysis.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rohrer and Baumann (2009)</a></cite> The MUV dataset contains 17 challenging tasks for around 90 thousand compounds and is specifically designed for validation of virtual screening techniques.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS9" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.9 </span>HIV</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The HIV dataset was introduced by the Drug Therapeutics Program (DTP) AIDS Antiviral Screen, which tested the ability to inhibit HIV replication for over 40,000 compounds.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">HIV ()</a></cite> Screening results were evaluated and placed into three categories: confirmed inactive (CI), confirmed active (CA) and confirmed moderately active (CM). We further combine the latter two labels, making it a classification task between inactive (CI) and active (CA and CM). As we are more interested in discover new categories of HIV inhibitors, scaffold splitting(introduced in the next subsection) is recommended for this dataset.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS10" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.10 </span>PDBbind</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS10.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS10.p1.1" class="ltx_p">PDBbind is a comprehensive database of experimentally measured binding affinities for bio-molecular complexes.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2004)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2005)</a></cite> Unlike other ligand-based biological activity datasets, in which only the structures of ligands are provided, PDBbind provides detailed 3D Cartesian coordinates of both ligands and their target proteins derived from experimental (e.g., X-Ray crystallography) measurements. The availability of coordinates of the protein-ligand complexes permits structure-based featurization that is aware of the protein-ligand binding geometry. We use the “refined” and “core” subsets of the database<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2014)</a></cite>, more carefully processed for data artifacts, as additional benchmarking targets. Samples in PDBbind dataset are collected over a relatively long period of time(since 1982), hence a time splitting pattern(introduced in the next subsection) is recommended to mimic actual development in the field.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS11" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.11 </span>BACE</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS11.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS11.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The BACE dataset provides quantitative (<math id="S3.SS1.SSS11.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="IC_{50}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>50</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">IC_{50}</annotation></semantics></math>) and qualitative (binary label) binding results for a set of inhibitors of human <math id="S3.SS1.SSS11.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>-secretase 1 (BACE-1)<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Subramanian et al. (2016)</a></cite>. All data are experimental values reported in scientific literature over the past decade, some with detailed crystal structures available. We merged a collection of 1522 compounds with their 2D structures and binary labels in MoleculeNet, built as a classification task. Similarly, regarding a single protein target, scaffold splitting will be more practically useful.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS12" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.12 </span>BBBP</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS12.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS12.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Blood-brain barrier penetration (BBBP) dataset comes from a recent study<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martins et al. (2012)</a></cite> on the modeling and prediction of the barrier permeability. As a membrane separating circulating blood and brain extracellular fluid, the blood-brain barrier blocks most drugs, hormones and neurotransmitters. Thus penetration of the barrier forms a long-standing issue in development of drugs targeting central nervous system. This dataset includes binary labels for over 2000 compounds on their permeability properties. Scaffold splitting is also recommended for this well-defined target.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS13" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.13 </span>Tox21</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS13.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS13.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The “Toxicology in the 21st Century” (Tox21) initiative created a public database measuring toxicity of compounds, which has been used in the 2014 Tox21 Data Challenge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tox ()</a></cite>. This dataset contains qualitative toxicity measurements for 8014 compounds on 12 different targets, including nuclear receptors and stress response pathways.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS14" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.14 </span>ToxCast</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS14.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS14.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ToxCast is another data collection (from the same initiative as Tox21) providing toxicology data for a large library of compounds based on <span id="S3.SS1.SSS14.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">in vitro</span> high-throughput screening.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Richard et al. (2016)</a></cite> The processed collection in MoleculeNet includes qualitative results of over 600 experiments on 8615 compounds.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS15" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.15 </span>SIDER</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS15.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS15.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Side Effect Resource (SIDER) is a database of marketed drugs and adverse drug reactions (ADR) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kuhn et al. (2016)</a></cite>. The version of the SIDER dataset in DeepChem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Altae-Tran et al. (2016)</a></cite> has grouped drug side-effects into 27 system organ classes following MedDRA classifications <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">med ()</a></cite> measured for 1427 approved drugs (following previous usage <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Altae-Tran et al. (2016)</a></cite>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS16" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.16 </span>ClinTox</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS16.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS16.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The ClinTox dataset, introduced as part of this work, compares drugs approved by the FDA and drugs that have failed clinical trials for toxicity reasons. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gayvert et al. (2016)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Artemov et al. (2016)</a></cite> The dataset includes two classification tasks for 1491 drug compounds with known chemical structures: (1) clinical trial toxicity (or absence of toxicity) and (2) FDA approval status. List of FDA-approved drugs are compiled from the SWEETLEAD database,<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Novick et al. (2013)</a></cite> and list of drugs that failed clinical trials for toxicity reasons are compiled from the Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov (AACT) database.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">AAC ()</a></cite></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Dataset splitting</h3>

<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/molnet_splits.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:238/278;" width="238" height="278" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Representation of Data Splits in MoleculeNet.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Typical machine learning methods require datasets to be split into training/validation/test subsets (or alternatively into <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-folds) for benchmarking. All MoleculeNet datasets are split into training, validation and test, following a 80/10/10 ratio. Training sets were used to train models, while validation sets were used for tuning hyperparameters, and test sets were used for evaluation of models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As mentioned previously, random splitting of molecular data isn’t always best for evaluating machine learning methods. Consequently, MoleculeNet implements multiple different splittings for each dataset. Random splitting randomly splits samples into the training/validation/test subsets. Scaffold splitting splits the samples based on their two-dimensional structural frameworks,<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bemis and Murcko (1996)</a></cite> as implemented in RDKit.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Landrum ()</a></cite> Since scaffold splitting attempts to separate structurally different molecules into different subsets, it offers a greater challenge for learning algorithms than the random split.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In addition, a stratified random sampling method is implemented on the QM7 dataset to reproduce the results from the original work.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Montavon et al. (2013)</a></cite> This method sorts datapoints in order of increasing label value (note this is only defined for real-valued output). This sorted list is then split into training/validation/test by ensuring that each set contains the full range of provided labels. Time splitting is also adopted for dataset that includes time information(PDBbind). Under this splitting method, model will be trained on older data and tested on newer data, mimicing real world development condition.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">MoleculeNet contributes the code for these splitting methods into DeepChem. Users of the library can use these splits on new datasets with short library calls.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Metrics</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MoleculeNet contains both regression datasets (QM7, QM7b, QM8, QM9, ESOL, FreeSolv, Lipophilicity and PDBbind) and classification datasets (PCBA, MUV, HIV, BACE, BBBP, Tox21, ToxCast and SIDER). Consequently, different performance metrics need to be measured for each. Following suggestions from the community<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain and Nicholls (2008)</a></cite>, regression datasets are evaluated by mean absolute error (MAE) and root-mean-square error (RMSE), classification datasets are evaluated by area under curve (AUC) of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hastie et al. (2009)</a></cite> and the precision recall curve (PRC)<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Davis and Goadrich (2006)</a></cite>. For datasets containing more than one task, we report the mean metric values over all tasks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/ROCvsPRC.png" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:238/314;" width="238" height="314" alt="Refer to caption">
