</table></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">* Number of positive samples/Number of negative samples</p>
</div></li>
</ul></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To allow better comparison, we propose regression metrics according to previous work on either same models or datasets. For classification datasets, we propose recommended metrics from the two commonly used metrics: AUC-PRC and AUC-ROC. Four representative sets of ROC curves and PRCs are depicted in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Metrics ‣ 3 Methods ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, resulting from the predictions of logistic regression and graph convolutional models on four tasks. Details about these tasks and AUC values of all curves are listed in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.3 Metrics ‣ 3 Methods ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Note that these four tasks have different class imbalances, represented as the number of positive samples and negative samples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As noted in previous literature<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Davis and Goadrich (2006)</a></cite>, ROC curves and PRCs are highly correlated, but perform significantly differently in case of high class imbalance. As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.3 Metrics ‣ 3 Methods ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, the fraction of positive samples decreases from over 80% (panels A and B) to less than 5% (panels G and H). This change accompanies the difference in how the two metrics treat model performances. In particular, PRCs put more emphasis on the low recall (also known as true positive rate (TPR)) side in case of highly imbalanced data: logistic regression slightly outperforms graph convolutional models in the low TPR side of ROC curves (panels C, E and G, lower left corner), which creates different margins on the low recall side of PRCs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">ROC curves and PRCs share one same axis, while using false positive rate (FPR) and precision for the other axis respectively. Recall that FPR and precision are defined as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\small FPR=\frac{\rm{False\,Positive}}{\rm{False\,Positive}+\rm{True\,Negative}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">R</mi></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">False</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">Positive</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">False</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">Positive</mi></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">True</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">Negative</mi></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\small FPR=\frac{\rm{False\,Positive}}{\rm{False\,Positive}+\rm{True\,Negative}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<table id="S3.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\small Precision=\frac{\rm{True\,Positive}}{\rm{False\,Positive}+\rm{True\,Positive}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">n</mi></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">True</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">Positive</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">False</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">Positive</mi></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">+</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">True</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">Positive</mi></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\small Precision=\frac{\rm{True\,Positive}}{\rm{False\,Positive}+\rm{True\,Positive}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">When positive samples form only a small proportion of all samples, false positive predictions exert a much greater influence on precision than FPR, amplifying the difference between PRC and ROC curves. Virtual screening experiments do have extremely low positive rates, suggesting that the correct metric to analyze may depend on the experiment at hand. In this work, we hence propose recommended metrics based on positive rates, PRC-AUC is used for datasets with positive rates less than 2%, otherwise ROC-AUC is used.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Featurization</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A core challenge for molecular machine learning is effectively encoding molecules into fixed-length strings or vectors. Although SMILES strings are unique representations of molecules, most molecular machine learning methods require further information to learn sophisticated electronic or topological features of molecules from limited amounts of data. (Recent work has demonstrated the ability to learn useful representations from SMILES strings using more sophisticated methods<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gómez-Bombarelli et al. (2016)</a></cite>, so it may be feasible to use SMILES strings for further learning tasks in the near future.) Furthermore, the enormity of chemical space often requires representations of molecules specifically suited to the learning task at hand. MoleculeNet contains implementations of six useful molecular featurization methods.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/molnet_feat.png" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:238/365;" width="238" height="365" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Diagrams of featurizations in MoleculeNet.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.4.1 </span>ECFP</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Extended-Connectivity Fingerprints (ECFP) are widely-used molecular characterizations in chemical informatics.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rogers and Hahn (2010)</a></cite> During the featurization process, a molecule is decomposed into submodules originated from heavy atoms, each assigned with a unique identifier. These segments and identifiers are extended through bonds to generate larger substructures and corresponding identifiers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">After hashing all these substructures into a fixed length binary fingerprint, the representation contains information about topological characteristics of the molecule, which enables it to be applied to tasks such as similarity searching and activity prediction. The MoleculeNet implementation uses ECFP4 fingerprints generated by RDKit.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Landrum ()</a></cite></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.4.2 </span>Coulomb Matrix</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Ab-initio</span> electronic structure calculations typically require a set of nuclear charges {<span id="S3.SS4.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Z</span>} and the corresponding Cartesian coordinates {<span id="S3.SS4.SSS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">R</span>} as input. The Coulomb Matrix (CM) <span id="S3.SS4.SSS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">M</span>, proposed by Rupp et al.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rupp et al. (2012)</a></cite> and defined below, encodes this information by use of the atomic self-energies and internuclear Coulomb repulsion operator.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_eqnarray ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle M_{IJ}=\begin{cases}0.5Z_{I}^{2.4}\qquad\mbox{for}\;I=J\\
\frac{Z_{I}Z_{J}}{|\bm{R}_{I}-\bm{R}_{J}|}\qquad\mbox{for}\;I\neq J\end{cases}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>Z</mi><mi>I</mi><mn>2.4</mn></msubsup></mrow><mspace style="width:2em;" width="2em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><mtext>for</mtext><mo lspace="0.280em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>J</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝑹</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝑹</mi><mi>J</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mspace style="width:2em;" width="2em"></mspace><mrow><mtext>for</mtext><mo lspace="0.280em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>≠</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle M_{IJ}=\begin{cases}0.5Z_{I}^{2.4}\qquad\mbox{for}\;I=J\\
\frac{Z_{I}Z_{J}}{|\bm{R}_{I}-\bm{R}_{J}|}\qquad\mbox{for}\;I\neq J\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Here, the off-diagonal elements correspond to the Coulomb repulsion between atoms I and J, and the diagonal elements correspond to a polynomial fit of atomic self-energy to nuclear charge. The Coulomb Matrix of a molecule is invariant to translation and rotation of that molecule, but not with respect to atom index permutation. In the construction of coulomb matrix, we first use the nuclear charges and distance matrix generated by RDKit<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Landrum ()</a></cite> to acquire the original coulomb matrix, then an optional random atom index sorting and binary expansion transformation can be applied during training in order to achieve atom index invariance, as reported by Montavon et al.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Montavon et al. (2013)</a></cite></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.4.3 </span>Grid Featurizer</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The grid featurizer is a featurization method (introduced in the current work) initially designed for the PDBBind dataset in which structural information of both the ligand and target protein are considered. Since binding affinity stems largely from the intermolecular forces between ligands and proteins, in addition to intramolecular interactions, we seek to incorporate both the chemical interaction within the binding pocket as well as features of the protein and ligand individually.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The grid featurizer was inspired by the NNscore featurizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Durrant and McCammon (2011)</a></cite> and SPLIF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Da and Kireev (2014)</a></cite> but optimized for speed, robustness, and generalizability. The intermolecular interactions enumerated by the featurizer include salt bridges and hydrogen bonding between protein and ligand, intra-ligand circular fingerprints, intra-protein circular fingerprints, and protein-ligand SPLIF fingerprints. A more detailed breakdown can be found in the appendix.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.4.4 </span>Symmetry Function</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Symmetry function, first introduced by Behler and Parrinello<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Behler and Parrinello (2007)</a></cite>, is another common encoding of atomic coordinates information. It focuses on preserving the rotational and permutation symmetry of the system. The local environment of an atom in the molecule is expressed as a series of radial and angular symmetry functions with different distance and angle cutoffs, the former focusing on distance between atom pairs and the latter focusing on angles formed within triplets of atoms.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As symmetry function put most emphasis on spatial positions of atoms, it is intrinsically hard for it to distinguish different atom types(H, C, O). MoleculeNet utilizes a slightly modified version of original symmetry function<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith et al. (2016)</a></cite> which further separate radial and angular symmetry terms according to the type of atoms in the pair or triplet. Further details can be found in the article<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith et al. (2016)</a></cite> or our implementation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS5" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.4.5 </span>Graph Convolutions</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The graph convolutions featurization support most graph-based models. It computes an initial feature vector and a neighbor list for each atom. The feature vector summarizes the atom’s local chemical environment, including atom-types, hybridization types, and valence structures. Neighbor lists represent connectivity of the whole molecule, which are further processed in each model to generate graph structures (discussed in further details in following parts).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS6" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.4.6 </span>Weave</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Similar to graph convolutions, the weave featurization encodes both local chemical environment and connectivity of atoms in a molecule. Atomic feature vectors are exactly the same, while connectivity uses more detailed pair features instead of neighbor listing. The weave featurization calculates a feature vector for each pair of atoms in the molecule, including bond properties (if directly connected), graph distance and ring info, forming a feature matrix. The method supports graph-based models that utilize properties of both nodes (atoms) and edges (bonds).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Models - Conventional Models</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MoleculeNet tests the performance of various machine learning models on the datasets discussed previously. These models could be further categorized into conventional method and graph-based method according to their structures and input types. The following sections will give brief introductions to benchmarked algorithms. The results section will discuss performance numbers in detail. Here we briefly review conventional methods including logistic regression, support vector classification, kernel ridge regression, random forests<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Breiman (2001)</a></cite>, gradient boosting<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Friedman (2001)</a></cite>, multitask networks<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramsundar et al. (2015)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. (2015)</a></cite>, bypass networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramsundar et al. ()</a></cite> and influence relevance voting<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Swamidass et al. (2009)</a></cite>. The next section graph-based models will give introductions to graph convolutional models<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duvenaud et al. (2015)</a></cite>, weave models<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kearnes et al. (2016)</a></cite>, directed acyclic graph models<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lusci et al. (2013)</a></cite>, deep tensor neural networks<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schütt et al. (2016)</a></cite>, ANI-1<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith et al. (2016)</a></cite> and message passing neural networks<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gilmer et al. (2017)</a></cite>. As part of this work, all methods are implemented in the open source DeepChem package<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">dee ()</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.5.1 </span>Logistic Regression</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Logistic regression models (Logreg) apply the logistic function to weighted linear combinations of their input features to obtain model predictions. It is often common to use regularization to encourage learned weights to be sparse. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Friedman et al. (2000)</a></cite> Note that logistic regression models are only defined for classification tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.5.2 </span>Support Vector Classification</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Support vector machine (SVM) is one of the most famous and widely-used machine learning method.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cortes and Vapnik (1995)</a></cite> As in classification task, it defines a decision plane which separates data points of different class with maximized margin. To further increase performance, we incorporates regularization and a radial basis function kernel (KernelSVM).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.5.3 </span>Kernel Ridge Regression</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Kernel ridge regression(KRR) is a combination of ridge regression and kernel trick. By using a nonlinear kernel function(radial basis function), it learns a non-linear function in the original space that maps features to predicted values.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.5.4 </span>Random Forests</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Random forests (RF) are ensemble prediction methods.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Breiman (2001)</a></cite> A random forest consists of many individual decision trees, each of which is trained on a subsampled version of the original dataset. The results for individual trees are averaged to provide output predictions for the full forest. Random forests can be used for both classification and regression tasks. Training a random forest can be computationally intensive, so benchmarks only include random forest results for smaller datasets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS5" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.5.5 </span>Gradient Boosting</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Gradient boosting is another ensemble method consisting of individual decision trees.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Friedman (2001)</a></cite> In contrast to random forests, it builds relatively simple trees which are sequentially incorporated to the ensemble. In each step, a new tree is generated in a greedy manner to minimize loss function. A sequence of such ”weak” trees are combined together into an additive model. We utilize the XGBoost implementation of gradient boosting in DeepChem.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen and Guestrin (2016)</a></cite></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS6" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.5.6 </span>Multitask/Singletask Network</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In a multitask network,<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramsundar et al. (2015)</a></cite> input featurizations are processed by fully connected neural network layers. The processed output is shared among all learning tasks in a dataset, and then fed into separate linear classifiers/regressors for each different task. In the case that a dataset contains only a single task, multitask networks are just fully connected neural networks(Singletask Network). Since multitask networks are trained on the joint data available for various tasks, the parameters of the shared layers are encouraged to produce a joint representation which can share information between learning tasks. This effect does seem to have limitations; merging data from uncorrelated tasks has only moderate effect.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kearnes et al. (2016)</a></cite> As a result, MoleculeNet does not attempt to train extremely large multitask networks combining all data for all datasets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS7" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.5.7 </span>Bypass Multitask Networks</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Multitask modeling relies on the fact that some features have explanatory power that is shared among multiple tasks. Note that the opposite may well be true; features useful for one task can be detrimental to other tasks. As a result, vanilla multitask networks can lack the power to explain unrelated variations in the samples. Bypass networks attempt to overcome this variation by merging in per-task independent layers that “bypass” shared layers to directly connect inputs with outputs.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramsundar et al. ()</a></cite> In other words, bypass multitask networks consist of <math id="S3.SS5.SSS7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\text{tasks}}+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>tasks</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\text{tasks}}+1</annotation></semantics></math> independent components: one “multitask” layers mapping all inputs to shared representations, and <math id="S3.SS5.SSS7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\text{tasks}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mtext>tasks</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\text{tasks}}</annotation></semantics></math> “bypass” layers mapping inputs for each specific task to their labels. As the two groups have separate parameters, bypass networks may have greater explanatory power than vanilla multitask networks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS8" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.5.8 </span>Influence Relevance Voting</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Influence Relevance Voting (IRV) systems are refined K-nearest neighbour classifiers.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Swamidass et al. (2009)</a></cite> Using the hypothesis that compounds with similar substructures have similar functionality, the IRV classifier makes its prediction by combining labels from the top-<math id="S3.SS5.SSS8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> compounds most similar to a provided test sample.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.SSS8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The Jaccard-Tanimoto similarity between fingerprints of compounds is used as the similarity measurement:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.SSS8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S(\vec{A},\vec{B})=\frac{A\cap B}{A\cup B}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∩</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S(\vec{A},\vec{B})=\frac{A\cap B}{A\cup B}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.SSS8.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS8.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Then IRV model calculates a weighted sum of labels of top K similar compounds to predict the result, in which weights are the outputs of a one-hidden layer neural network with similarities and rankings of top-<math id="S3.SS5.SSS8.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> compounds as input. Detailed descriptions of the model can be found in the original article.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Swamidass et al. (2009)</a></cite></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.6 </span>Models - Graph Based Models</h3>

<div id="S3.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Early attempts to directly use molecular structures instead of selected features has emerged in 1990s<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baskin et al. (1997)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kireev (1995)</a></cite>. While in recent years, models propelled by the very similar idea start to grow rapidly. These specifically designed methods, namely graph-based models, are naturally suitable for modelling molecules. By defining atoms as nodes, bonds as edges, molecules can be modeled as mathematical graphs. As noted in a recent paper<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gilmer et al. (2017)</a></cite>, this natural similarity has inspired a number of models to utilize the graph structure of molecules to gain higher performances. In general, graph-based models apply adaptive functions to nodes and edges, allowing for a learnable featurization process. MoleculeNet provides implementations of multiple graph-based models which use different variants of molecular graphs. We describe these methods in the following sections. Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 3.6 Models - Graph Based Models ‣ 3 Methods ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> provide simple illustrations of these methods’ core structures.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/model_structure.png" id="S3.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/239;" width="476" height="239" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Core structures of graph-based models implemented in MoleculeNet. To build features for the central dark green atom: <span id="S3.F6.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span> Graph Convolutional Model: features are updated by combination with neighbour atoms; <span id="S3.F6.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">B</span> Directed Acyclic Graph Model: all bonds are directed towards the central atom, features are propagated from the farthest atom to the central atom through directed bonds; <span id="S3.F6.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">C</span> Weave Model: Pairs are formed between each pair of atoms(including not directly bonded pairs), features for the central atom are updated using all other atoms and their corresponding pairs, pair features are also updated by combination of the two pairing atoms; <span id="S3.F6.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">D</span> Message Passing Neural Network: Neighbour atoms’ features are input into bondtype-dependent neural networks, forming outputs(messages). Features of the central atom are then updated using the outputs; <span id="S3.F6.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">E</span> Deep Tensor Neural Network: No explicit bonding information is included, features are updated using all other atoms based on their corresponding physical distances; <span id="S3.F6.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">F</span> ANI-1: features are built on distance information between pairs of atoms(radial symmetry functions) and angular information between triplets of atoms(angular symmetry functions).</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.6.1 </span>Graph Convolutional models</h4>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Graph convolutional models (GC) extend the decomposition principles of circular fingerprints. Both methods gradually merge information for distant atoms by extending radially through bonds. This information is used to generate identifiers for all substructures. However, instead of applying fixed hash functions, graph convolutional models allow for adaptive learning by using differentiable network layers. This creates a learnable process capable of extracting useful representations of molecules suited to the task at hand. (Note that this property is shared, to some degree, by all deep architectures considered in MoleculeNet. However, graph convolutional architectures are more explicitly designed to encourage extraction of useful featurizations).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS6.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">On a higher level, graph convolutional models treat molecules as undirected graphs, and apply the same learnable function to every node (atom) and its neighbors (bonded atoms) in the graph. This structure recapitulates convolution layers in visual recognition deep networks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS6.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">MoleculeNet uses the graph convolutional implementation in DeepChem from previous work.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Altae-Tran et al. (2016)</a></cite> This implementation converts SMILES strings into molecular graphs using RDKit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Landrum ()</a></cite> As mentioned previously, the initial representations assign to each atom a vector of features including its element, connectivity, valence, etc. Then several graph convolutional modules, each consisting of a graph convolutional layer, a batch normalization layer and a graph pool layer, are sequentially added, followed by a fully-connected dense layer. Finally, the feature vectors for all nodes (atoms) are summed, generating a graph feature vector, which is fed to a classification or regression layer.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.6.2 </span>Weave models</h4>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Weave architecture is another graph-based model that regards each molecule as a undirected graph. Similar to graph convolutional models, it utilizes the idea of adaptive learning on extracting meaningful representations.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kearnes et al. (2016)</a></cite> The major difference is the size of the convolutions: To update features of an atom, weave models combine info from all other atoms and their corresponding pairs in the molecule. Weave models are more efficient at transmitting information between distant atoms, at the price of increased complexity for each convolution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS6.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In our implementation, a molecule is first encoded into a list of atomic features and a matrix of pair features by the weave model’s featurization method. Then in each weave module, these features are inputted into four sets of fully connected layers (corresponding to four paths from two original features to two updated features) and concatenated to form new atomic and pair features. After stacking several weave modules, a similar gather layer combines atomic features together to form molecular features that are fed into task-specific layers.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.6.3 </span>Directed Acyclic Graph models</h4>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) models regard molecules as directed graphs. While chemical bonds typically do not have natural directions, one can arbitrarily generate a DAG on a molecule by designating a central atom and then define directions of all bonds in certain orientations towards the atom.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lusci et al. (2013)</a></cite> In the case of small molecules, taking all possible orientations is computationally feasible. In other words, for a molecule with <math id="S3.SS6.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> atoms, the model will generate <math id="S3.SS6.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> DAGs, each centered on a different atom.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS6.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the actual calculations of a graph, a vector of graph features is calculated for each atom based on its atomic features (reusing the graph convolutions featurizer) and its parents’ graph features. As features gradually propagate through bonds, information converges on the central atom. Then a final sum of all graphs gives the molecular features, which are fed into classification or regression tasks. Note that <math id="S3.SS6.SSS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> graphs are evaluated for each molecule, which can cause a significant increase in required calculations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.6.4 </span>Deep Tensor Neural Networks</h4>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Deep Tensor Neural Networks (DTNN) are adaptable extensions of the Coulomb Matrix featurizer.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schütt et al. (2016)</a></cite> The core idea is to directly use nuclear charge (atom number) and the distance matrix to predict energetic, electronic or thermodynamic properties of small molecules. To build a learnable system, the model first maps atom numbers to trainable embeddings(randomly initialized) as atomic features. Then each atomic feature <math id="S3.SS6.SSS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is updated based on distance info <math id="S3.SS6.SSS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math> and other atomic features <math id="S3.SS6.SSS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>. Comparing with Weave models, DTNNs share the same idea in terms of updating based on both atomic and pair features, while the difference is using physical distance instead of graph distance. Note that the use of 3D coordinates to calculate physical distances limits DTNNs to quantum mechanical (or perhaps biophysical) datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS6.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We reimplement the model proposed by Schütt et al.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schütt et al. (2016)</a></cite> in a more generalized fashion. Atom numbers and a distance matrix are calculated by RDKit<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Landrum ()</a></cite>, using the Coulomb matrix featurizer. After embedding atom numbers into feature vectors <math id="S3.SS6.SSS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, we update <math id="S3.SS6.SSS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> in each convolutional layer by adding the outputs from all network layers which use <math id="S3.SS6.SSS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS6.SSS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S3.SS6.SSS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\neq j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\neq j</annotation></semantics></math>) as input. After several layers of convolutions, all atomic features are summed together to form molecular features, used for classification and regression tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS5" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.6.5 </span>ANI-1</h4>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ANI-1 is designed as a deep neural network capable of learning accurate and transferable potentials for organic molecules. It is based on the symmetry function method<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Behler and Parrinello (2007)</a></cite>, with additional changes enabling it to learn different potentials for different atom types. Feature vector, a series of symmetry functions, is built for each atom in the molecule based on its atom type and interaction with other atoms. Then the feature vectors are fed into different neural network potentials(depending on atom types) to generate predictions of properties.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS6.SSS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This model is first introduced by Smith et al.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith et al. (2016)</a></cite>. In their original article, the model is trained on  58k small molecules with 8 or less heavy atoms, each with multiple poses and potentials. Training set in total has  17.2 million data points, which is far bigger than qm8 or qm9 in our collection. Since we only have molecules in their most stable configuration, we cannot expect similar level of accuracy. Further comparison and benchmarking with similar size of training set is left to future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6.SSS6" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.6.6 </span>Message Passing Neural Networks</h4>

<div id="S3.SS6.SSS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Message passing neural network(MPNN) is a generalized model proposed by Gilmer et al.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gilmer et al. (2017)</a></cite> that targets to formulate a single framework for graph based model. The prediction process is separated into two phases: message passing phase and readout phase. Multiple message passing phases are stacked to extract abstract information of the graph, then the readout phase is responsible for mapping the graph to its properties.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS6.SSS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.SSS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Here we reimplemented the best-performing model in the original article: using an Edge network as message passing function and a set2set model<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vinyals et al. (2015)</a></cite> as readout function. In message passing phase, an edge-dependent neural network maps all neighbour atoms’ feature vectors to updating messages, which are then merged using gated recurrent units. In the final readout phase, feature vectors for all atoms are regarded as a set, then an LSTM using attention mechanism is applied on the set for multiple steps, with its final state used as the output for the molecule.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Results and Discussion</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we discuss the performance of benchmarked models on MoleculeNet datasets. Different models are applied depending on the size, features and task types of the dataset. All graph models use their corresponding featurizations. Non-graph models use ECFP featurizations by default, Coulomb Matrix (CM) and Grid featurizer are also applied for certain datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We run a brief Gaussian process hyperparameter optimization on each combination of dataset and model. Then three independent runs with different random seeds are performed. More detailed description of optimization method and performance tables can be found in appendix. Note that all benchmark results presented here are the average of three runs, with standard deviations listed or illustrated as error bars.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We also run a set of experiments focusing on how variable size of training set affect model performances.(Tox21, FreeSolv and QM7) Details will be presented in the following texts.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Physiology and Biophysics Tasks</h3>

<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/Biophysics.png" id="S4.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/390;" width="476" height="390" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Benchmark performances for biophysics tasks: <span id="S4.F7.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PCBA</span>, 4 models are evaluated by AUC-PRC on random split; <span id="S4.F7.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MUV</span>, 8 models are evaluated by AUC-PRC on random split; <span id="S4.F7.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">HIV</span>, 8 models are evaluated by AUC-ROC on scaffold split; <span id="S4.F7.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BACE</span>, 9 models are evaluated by AUC-ROC on scaffold split. For AUC-ROC and AUC-PRC, higher value indicates better performance(to the right).</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F8" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/Physiology.png" id="S4.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/401;" width="476" height="401" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>Benchmark performances for physiology tasks: <span id="S4.F8.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ToxCast</span>, 8 models are evaluated by AUC-ROC on random split; <span id="S4.F8.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tox21</span>, 9 models are evaluated by AUC-ROC on random split; <span id="S4.F8.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BBBP</span>, 9 models are evaluated by AUC-ROC on scaffold split; <span id="S4.F8.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SIDER</span>, 9 models are evaluated by AUC-ROC on random split. For AUC-ROC, higher value indicates better performance(to the right).</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/Physiology2.png" id="S4.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:238/222;" width="238" height="222" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>Benchmark performances for physiology tasks: <span id="S4.F9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ClinTox</span>, 9 models are evaluated by AUC-ROC on random split.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tables <a href="#S6.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 6.2 Performances ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, <a href="#S6.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 6.2 Performances ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> and Figures <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.1 Physiology and Biophysics Tasks ‣ 4 Results and Discussion ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, <a href="#S4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 4.1 Physiology and Biophysics Tasks ‣ 4 Results and Discussion ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, <a href="#S4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 4.1 Physiology and Biophysics Tasks ‣ 4 Results and Discussion ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> report AUC-ROC or AUC-PRC results of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9</annotation></semantics></math> different models on biophysics datasets (PCBA, MUV, HIV, BACE) and physiology datasets (BBBP, Tox21, Toxcast, SIDER, ClinTox). Some models were too computationally expensive to be run on the larger datasets. All of these datasets contain only classification tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Most models have train scores (listed in Tables <a href="#S6.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 6.2 Performances ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, <a href="#S6.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 6.2 Performances ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>) higher than validation/test scores, indicating that overfitting is a general issue. Singletask logistic regression exhibits the largest gaps between train scores and validation/test scores, while models incorporating multitask structure generally show less overfit, suggesting that multitask training has a regularizing effect. Most physiological and biophysical datasets in MoleculeNet have only a low volume of data for each task. Multitask algorithms combine different tasks, resulting in a larger pool of data for model training. In particular, multitask training can, to some extent, compensate for the limited data amount available for each individual task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Graph convolutional models and weave models, each based on an adaptive method of featurization<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duvenaud et al. (2015)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kearnes et al. (2016)</a></cite>, show strong validation/test results on larger datasets, along with less overfit. Similar results are reported in previous graph-based algorithms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kearnes et al. (2016)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duvenaud et al. (2015)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gilmer et al. (2017)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schütt et al. (2016)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lusci et al. (2013)</a></cite>, showing that learnable featurizations can provide a large boost compared with conventional featurizations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For smaller singletask datasets (less than 3000 samples), differences between models are less clear. Kernel SVM and ensemble tree methods (gradient boosting and random forests) are more robust under data scarcity, while they generally need longer running time (see Table <a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 6.1.14 ANI-1 ‣ 6.1 Model Training and Hyperparameter Optimization ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). Worse performances of graph-based models are within expectation as complex models generally require more training data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Bypass networks show higher train scores and equal or higher validation/test scores compared with vanilla multitask networks, suggesting that the bypass structure does add robustness. IRV models achieve performance broadly comparable with multitask networks. However, the quadratic nearest neighbor search makes the IRV models slower to train than the multitask networks (see Table <a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 6.1.14 ANI-1 ‣ 6.1 Model Training and Hyperparameter Optimization ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Three datasets (HIV, BACE, BBBP) in these two categories are evaluated under scaffold splitting. As compounds are divided by their molecular scaffolds, increasing differences between train, validation and test performances are observed. Scaffold splits provide a stronger test of a given model’s generalizability compared with random splitting. Two datasets (PCBA, MUV) are evaluated by AUC-PRC, which is more practically useful under high class imbalance as discussed above. Graph convolutional model performs the best on PCBA (positive rate <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.40\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.40</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.40\%</annotation></semantics></math>), while results on MUV (positive rate <math id="S4.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.20\%</annotation></semantics></math>) are much less stable, which is most likely due to its extreme low amount of positive samples. Under such high imbalance, graph-based models are still not robust enough in controlling false positives.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/Tox21_variable.png" id="S4.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/292;" width="381" height="292" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Out-of-sample performances with different training set sizes on Tox21. Each datapoint is the average of 5 independent runs, with standard deviations shown as error bars.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Here we performed a more detailed experiment to illustrate how model performances change with increasing training samples. We trained multiple models on Tox21 with training sets of different size(<math id="S4.SS1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the whole dataset) Figure <a href="#S4.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 4.1 Physiology and Biophysics Tasks ‣ 4 Results and Discussion ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> displayed mean out-of-sample performances (and standard deviations) of five independent runs. A clear increase on performance is observed for each model, and graph-based models (Graph convolutional model and weave model) always stay on top of the lines. By drawing a horizontal line at around 0.80, we can see graph-based models achieve the similar level of accuracy with multitask networks by using only one-third of the training samples(<math id="S4.SS1.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\%</annotation></semantics></math> versus <math id="S4.SS1.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\%</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Biophysics Task - PDBbind</h3>

<figure id="S4.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/PDBbind.png" id="S4.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:238/529;" width="238" height="529" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span>Benchmark performances of <span id="S4.F11.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PDBbind</span>: 5 models are evaluated by RMSE on the three subsets: core, refined and full. Time split is applied to all three subsets. Noe that for RMSE, lower value indicates better performance(to the right).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The PDBBind dataset maps distinct ligand-protein structures to their binding affinities. As discussed in the datasets section, we created grid featurizer to harness the joint ligand-protein structural information in PDBBind to build a model that predicts the experimental <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> of binding. We applied time splitting to all three subsets: core, refined, and full subsets of PDBbind(Core contains roughly 200 structures, refined 4000, and full 15000. The smaller datasets are cleaned more thoroughly than larger datasets.), with all results displayed in Table <a href="#S6.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 6.2 Performances ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S4.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ 4.2 Biophysics Task - PDBbind ‣ 4 Results and Discussion ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>. Clearly as dataset size increased, we can see a significant boost on validation/test set performances. At the same time, for the two larger subsets: refined and full, switching from pure ligand-based ECFP to grid featurizer do increase the performances by a small margin in both Singletask networks and random forests. While for core subset, all models are showing relatively high errors and two featurizations do not show clear differences, which is within expectation as sample amount in core subset is too small to support a stable model performance. Note that models on the full set aren’t significantly superior to models with less data; this effect may be due to the additional data being less clean.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Note that all models display heavy overfitting. Additional clean data may be required to create more accurate models for protein-ligand binding.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Physical Chemistry Tasks</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Solubility, solvation free energy and lipophilicity are basic physical chemistry properties important for understanding how molecules interact with solvents. Figure <a href="#S4.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ 4.3 Physical Chemistry Tasks ‣ 4 Results and Discussion ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> and Table <a href="#S6.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 6.2 Performances ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> presented performances on predicting these properties.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Graph-based methods: graph convolutional model, DAG, MPNN and weave model all exhibit significant boosts over vanilla singletask network, indicating the advantages of learnable featurizations. Differences between graph-based methods are rather minor and task-specific. The best-performing models in this category can already reach the accuracy level of <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ab-initio</span> predictions(+/- 0.5 for ESOL, +/- 1.5 kcal/mol for FreeSolv).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We performed a more detailed comparison between data-driven methods and <span id="S4.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ab-initio</span> calculations on FreeSolv. Hydration free energy has been widely used as a test of computational chemistry methods. With free energy values ranging from <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-25.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>25.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-25.5</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.4\mbox{kcal/mol}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>kcal/mol</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.4\mbox{kcal/mol}</annotation></semantics></math> in the FreeSolv dataset, RMSE for calculated results reach up to <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.5\mbox{kcal/mol}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.5</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>kcal/mol</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5\mbox{kcal/mol}</annotation></semantics></math>.<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mobley et al. (2014)</a></cite> On the other hand, though machine learning methods typically need large amounts of training data to acquire predictive power, they can achieve higher accuracies given enough data. We investigate how the performance of machine learning methods on FreeSolv changes with the volume of training data. In particular, we want to know the amount of data required for machine learning to achieve accuracy similar to that of physically inspired algorithms.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F12" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/FreeSolv_variable.png" id="S4.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/292;" width="381" height="292" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 12: </span>Out-of-sample performances with different training set sizes on FreeSolv. Each datapoint is the average of 5 independent runs, with standard deviations shown as error bars.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For Figure <a href="#S4.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ 4.3 Physical Chemistry Tasks ‣ 4 Results and Discussion ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, we similarly generated a series of models with different training set volumes and calculated their out-of-sample RMSE. Each data point displayed is the average of 5 independent runs, with standard deviations displayed as error bars. Both graph convolutional model and weave model are capable of achieving better performances with enough training samples (<math id="S4.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the data respectively). Given the size of FreeSolv dataset is only around 600 compounds, a weave model can reach state-of-the-art free energy calculation performances by training on merely 200 samples. On the other hand, comparing with singletask network’s performance, weave model achieved the same level of accuracy with only one-third of the training samples.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F13" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/PhysicalChemistryTasks.png" id="S4.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:238/578;" width="238" height="578" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 13: </span>Benchmark performances for physical chemistry tasks: <span id="S4.F13.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ESOL</span>, 8 models are evaluated by RMSE on random split; <span id="S4.F13.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">FreeSolv</span>, 8 models are evaluated by RMSE on random split; <span id="S4.F13.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lipophilicity</span>, 8 models are evaluated by RMSE on random split. Note that for RMSE, lower value indicates better performance(to the right).</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Quantum Mechanics Tasks</h3>

<figure id="S4.F14" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/QM.png" id="S4.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:205/575;" width="205" height="575" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 14: </span>Benchmark performances for quantum mechanics tasks: <span id="S4.F14.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">QM7</span>, 8 models are evaluated by MAE on stratified split; <span id="S4.F14.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">QM7b</span>, 3 models (QM7b only provides 3D coordinates) are evaluated by MAE on random split; <span id="S4.F14.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">QM8</span>, 7 models are evaluated by MAE on random split; <span id="S4.F14.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">QM9</span>, 5 models are evaluated by MAE on random split. Note that for MAE, lower value indicates better performance(to the right)</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The QM datasets (QM7, QM7b, QM8, QM9) represent another distinct category of properties that are typically calculated through solving Schrödinger’s equation (approximately using techniques such as DFT). As most conventional methods are slower than data-driven methods by orders of magnitude, we hope to learn effective approximators by training on existing datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S6.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ 6.2 Performances ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S4.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ 4.4 Quantum Mechanics Tasks ‣ 4 Results and Discussion ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> display the performances in mean absolute error of multiple methods. Table <a href="#S6.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ 6.2 Performances ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, <a href="#S6.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ 6.2 Performances ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> and <a href="#S6.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ 6.2 Performances ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> show detailed performances for each task.(Due to difference in range of labels, mean performances of QM7b and QM9 are more skewed) Unsurprisingly, significant boosts on performances and less overfitting are observed for models incorporating distance information (multitask networks and KRR with Coulomb Matrix featurization, DTNN, MPNN). In particular, KRR and multitask networks(CM) outperform their corresponding baseline models in QM7 and QM9 by a large margin, while DTNN and MPNN display less error comparing with graph convolutional models as well. At the same time, DTNN and MPNN gains better performances than multitask networks and KRR (CM) on most tasks. Table <a href="#S6.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ 6.2 Performances ‣ 6 Appendix ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> shows that DTNN outperforms KRR(CM) on 12/14 tasks in QM7b(Though the mean error shows the opposite result due to averaging errors on different magnitudes). In total, DTNN and MPNN covers the best-performing models on 28/39 of all tasks in this category, again reflecting the superiority of learnable featurization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Another variable trainging size experiment is performed on QM7: predicting atomization energy. All mean absolute error performances are displayed in Figure <a href="#S4.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ 4.4 Quantum Mechanics Tasks ‣ 4 Results and Discussion ‣ MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>. Clearly incorporation of spatial position creates the huge gap between models, DTNN and multitask networks(CM) reach similar level of accuracy as reported in previous work on this dataset. (There is still a gap between the MoleculeNet implementation and best reported numbers from previous work<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Montavon et al. (2013)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schütt et al. (2016)</a></cite>, which would likely be closed by training models longer). ANI-1 is also reported to achieve comparable performances on similar task in the previous work<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith et al. (2016)</a></cite> with a much larger dataset. Apparently its worse performance is restricted by training set size, as the MAE is keep decreasing with more training samples.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F15" class="ltx_figure"><img src="1703.00564v2/QM7_variable.png" id="S4.F15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/292;" width="381" height="292" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 15: </span>Out-of-sample performances with different training set sizes on QM7. Each datapoint is the average of 5 independent runs, with standard deviations shown as error bars.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For QM series, proper choice of featurization appears critical. As mentioned previously, ECFP only consider graph substructures, while Coulomb Matrix and graph featurizations used by DTNN and MPNN are explicitly calculated on charges and physical distances, which are exactly the required input for solving Schrödinger’s equation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<span id="S5.T3.2.1.1.18.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">GC: 0.638</span></span>
